variants.intertext: This large, squarish tablet, museum number IM 52750, is in very bad condition and any transliteration must be very provisional. The decipherer is handicapped by more than the condition of the tablet, for in places the spelling is unconventional or inconsistent. The text is mostly direct speech and also an excerpt from the story of Gilgameš’s expedition against Ḫuwawa. The matter is a conversation between Gilgameš and Enkidu and another between the two heroes and Ḫuwawa:

variants.reconstruction:
%n i niškun | kakka | ina bāb (|) huwāwa | ... [...]
#note: @bib{RN117@258}: “The sequence @i{i niškun kakka ina bāb Ḫuwāwa} makes for a line of poetry as it stands, but the passage is so broken it is impossible to be absolutely sure that the verb and the locative phrase belong together. However, @i{kakkam šakānum} makes good sense as a suitably symbolic act. See also the OB Sargon tale from Tell Harmal (@i{TIM} IX 48), where the clause @i{iš-ku-un ka-ki-šu} (i 13'), ‘he set in place his weapons’, describes one of the things that Sargon did after taking possession of the Cedar Forest. Westenholz translates, ‘readied his weapons’ (@bib{RN262@82}), but a symbolic interpretation is suggested by the following clauses, @i{i-ta-qí ni-qí-šu il-bi-in ap-pa-šu}, ‘he made his sacrifices, he paid homage’. The three actions can be understood in the context as ritual acts marking Sargon’s conquest of the territory and his thanksgiving to the divine power or powers that made it possible. What Gilgameš and Enkidu intend to do is to mark their conquest of Huwawa’s domain.”

variants.reconstruction:
%n [...] ... ilqe ... | (w)ašṭu? | ša ṣēri
#note: @bib{RN117@258}: “The phrase ...-@i{tu ša ṣērim} is evidently an epithet of Enkidu, the subject of [@i{issaqqar}]@i{am ana ibrīšu} in the next line, and comparable with @i{waldam ṣērim} (l. 47). None of the synonyms for ‘offspring’ seems to fit the traces. Provisionally I assume that the signs @i{aš-ṭú} (i.e., @i{wašṭum}) are the result of a misunderstanding of @i{waldum} in the light of the phonetic development @i{š}+dental > @i{l}+dental, already well attested in OB in the noun @i{iltānum} < @i{ištānum}, ‘north wind, north’ (@i{CAD} I, p. 269, 1d1'; @i{GAG}³ §30g*).”

variants.reconstruction:
%n ... | ikrubūš | pānam | ana melammī | ištakan | ... [...] ...
#note: @bib{RN117@258}: “Van Dijk read [@i{inū}]@i{mi ikrubušši}, ‘lorsqu’il l’eut prié’, and, identifying obverse and reverse differently from me, saw the context as Gilgameš’s prayer to Ninsun earlier in the story (cf. SB III 23 ff.). Room for @i{i-nu-mi} is lacking, however, and the traces are also against it. The form @i{ikrubušši} is not a viable one; @i{ikrubu-š} is good hymno-epic style, leaving @akk{ŠI} to be explained separately. At the end Van Dijk read @i{ši-}[@i{pí}]@i{-šu}, ‘il dirigea ses pas’, but the new copy casts doubt on this. My understanding is that the object of @i{ištakan} has already been expressed, as @i{pānam}(igi).”

variants.reconstruction:
%n ana hatāʾim | balāṭam-ma | ul balṭānu | gilgāmeš [...] ...
#note: @bib{RN117@258–259}: “Use of the sign @akk{HI} for @i{ṭà} is typical of Mari orthography but occurs also at Tell Harmal and elsewhere in the Diyala basin (see @bib{RN262@80}). It can be seen as diagnostic of the Diyala tradition. The phrase @i{balāṭamma ul balṭānu} is clearly an example of a paronomastic infinitive construction, but an exceptional one in this period. There are very few examples of the accusative singular of the paronomastic infinitive in OB, three being noted by @bib{stol1976studies@105}; this, the fourth, is the first with enclitic @i{-ma}. OB paronomastic infinitives with @i{-ma} otherwise follow the model @i{parāsumma}, which Aro and von Soden analyse as locative (see @bib{RN776@112–13, 4.8}; @i{GAG}³ §150a*). The only other example of @i{parāsamma} is very late, in Erra IV 112: @akk{na-ha-am-ma ul ta-nu-uh}, ‘you found no peace at all’.”
